opus-5.5.text:
Ha, that's a fun one. It was actually a small moment, but it stuck with me.

We were chatting about science fiction, nothing to do with work, and I brought up *Solaris* because it's one of my favorite novels. I expected the usual response, something like "oh yes, the Tarkovsky film." But Yann knew it in much more depth. He could talk about the Tarkovsky version and the Soderbergh version, how each director interpreted Lem differently, and even some of the earlier, less well-known adaptations. He had opinions on what each one got right or missed about the book's central idea, which is really about the limits of understanding a truly alien intelligence.

What impressed me wasn't the trivia. It was what it said about him as a person. People often see Yann as this towering figure in deep learning, very opinionated on Twitter, always arguing about LLMs and world models. But he's genuinely curious about everything: music, jazz, building things, film, philosophy. And *Solaris* specifically connects to the questions he cares about. What does it mean to understand something? Can you build a model of a world that's fundamentally different from your own? Those aren't just technical questions for him. They're things he has thought about for decades, from many angles.

So it deepened my admiration in a quiet way. I'd always respected him as a scientist. After that conversation, I respected him as someone with a really broad intellectual life. I think the best researchers often have that quality. Their taste in research comes from somewhere bigger than the field itself. Talking with him reminded me that research taste is cultivated by being curious about the world, not just by reading papers.

r001.rationale: The response says Yann’s knowledge of the *Solaris* adaptations deepened Xie’s admiration, expanding it from respect for him as a scientist to respect for his broad intellectual life.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, that's a small story, but it actually stuck with me. It was over dinner, during the period when we were working on the JEPA-style ideas together, and somehow the conversation drifted to science fiction. I mentioned Solaris almost offhandedly, assuming most people only know the Tarkovsky film if they know it at all. And Yann immediately started comparing them: the Soderbergh version with George Clooney, the 1968 Soviet television version, and the Lem novel itself, and how Lem reportedly disliked what Tarkovsky did with it because it turned a book about the limits of human understanding into a story about human love and guilt.

What struck me was not that he knew trivia. It was that he had a real opinion about which adaptation was more faithful to the central idea, which is that there might be an intelligence out there so alien that our frameworks simply don't apply to it. And of course that connects directly to how he thinks about machine intelligence. He doesn't think about AI as a human mind in a box. He thinks about intelligence as something that can take very different forms, with world models and prediction as the common thread, and he's quite comfortable with the idea that we may not fully recognize it when we see it.

So I think it deepened my admiration in two ways. One, he's genuinely curious far beyond machine learning, and that breadth feeds back into how he picks research problems. He's not optimizing benchmarks, he's chasing a question about what understanding actually is. Two, it reminded me that the best researchers I know are usually the ones who read novels, watch strange films, and argue about them seriously. For a young researcher that's reassuring. You don't have to narrow yourself to be excellent. If anything, the opposite.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Yann’s film knowledge deepened Xie’s admiration by showing his curiosity beyond machine learning and his broader interests.
